opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing about BFF is that it starts with no purpose whatsoever. You have a "soup" of short tapes, just random bytes, and the instruction set is a minimal variant of Brainfuck where the code and the data live on the same tape. At each step you pick two tapes at random, stick them together, run the result for a limited number of steps, and then pull them apart again. There's no fitness function and no reward. Nobody tells the system what to do. For a long while, nothing much happens. It's noise.

Then, at some point, there's something like a phase transition. Self-replicating programs appear, and they rapidly take over the soup. You can see it in the measures. The compressibility of the soup shoots up, and the number of operations being executed per interaction jumps dramatically. Suddenly the system is doing a great deal of computation, where before it was doing almost none.

The question of purpose comes in because, once you have a replicator, you can meaningfully say that parts of the program are *for* something. This instruction is there in order to copy that region. This loop exists in order to make the tape reproduce. Before the transition, it makes no sense to ask what a particular byte is for. After it, the question has an answer. Function has emerged from dynamics. I don't think that's a metaphor or a projection on our part. It's a real change in the kind of thing that's there. The replicator persists because of what it does, and that's what purpose minimally means.

What I find most striking is how the replicators arise. Mostly it isn't random mutation slowly hill-climbing toward a copier. Mutation actually turns out not to be necessary. What drives it is fusion. Little fragments that each do some partial thing, maybe copying a byte or moving a head, get combined through these interactions. Collectively they form something that reproduces better than any of its parts. That's symbiogenesis, the same story Lynn Margulis told about mitochondria and eukaryotic cells. Complexity grows by things merging into larger cooperative wholes, which then become new units of selection.

So my view is that purpose isn't some extra ingredient you have to add to physics. It's what you get when you have a dynamically stable system that maintains and reproduces itself through computation. Life is computational in that sense: to copy yourself, you have to embody a program that builds you. Once that loop closes, "wanting" to persist isn't mysterious anymore. Things that don't act as if they want to persist simply aren't around to be observed. Purpose is a kind of self-fulfilling prophecy written in dynamics.

And this scales up. The same logic of functional parts combining into larger functional wholes runs from replicators to cells to multicellular organisms, to societies, and arguably to the AI systems we're building now. Each level involves new kinds of purposes that can't be reduced to the purposes of the parts, even though nothing magical was added along the way.

r002.rationale: It describes random-byte tapes repeatedly being joined and run, after which self-replicating programs appear.

r003.rationale: It identifies making the tape reproduce as the replicator’s purpose.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the thing that I think is really surprising about the BFF experiment, and the reason I keep coming back to it, is that it's a system with essentially nothing in it. There's no fitness function. There's no reward. Nobody tells it what to do. You just have this soup of random tapes, random bytes, 64 bytes each, and they interact in pairs. Two tapes get concatenated, you run the result as a little Brainfuck-like program, you split it back apart, and that's it. Plus a trickle of mutation. That's the whole thing.

And for a long time, nothing happens. You just see noise. The entropy of the soup stays maximal. And then, at some point, there's a transition, and suddenly the soup is full of self-replicators. Programs that copy themselves. And they're everywhere, and the entropy collapses, and from then on you have something that looks a lot like evolution: lineages, variation, competition, programs that get better at copying, programs that parasitize other programs.

Now, where does the purpose come in? I think the key move is to notice that nobody put it there. We did not define "copy yourself" as a goal. We didn't select for it. What happened is that in a world where things are getting randomly overwritten all the time, a pattern that happens to reproduce itself is a pattern that persists. And a pattern that persists is a pattern that's still around to be observed. So replication is in some sense the only thing that can happen, if anything is going to happen at all. Everything else washes out.

And once you have that, you have something that looks like purpose. A replicator "wants" to copy itself, in the sense that it does things that are organized around that outcome, and if it fails it ceases to exist. That's the origin of teleology, as far as I'm concerned. It's not that purpose was injected from the outside. It's that there's a dynamic, a kind of selection on existence itself, which makes the stuff that's around look purposive. Function and purpose are what you get when you look at a system through the lens of what it has to do in order to still be there.

What I find philosophically interesting is that this happens before Darwinian evolution in the usual sense. People often think of natural selection as the thing that generates purpose. But in BFF, you don't get natural selection until you already have replicators with heritable variation. So there's a prior step, which is just: of all the possible configurations of bytes, which ones are dynamically stable? And it turns out the stable ones are the self-perpetuating ones. Purpose is kind of baked into that stability.

And I think it also tells us something about computation. Because the only reason this works at all is that the tapes are programs. They can act on each other. It's not a chemistry in the usual sense; it's interactions that are Turing-complete. And I suspect that's what life is, fundamentally. It's computation that has figured out how to keep itself going. Once you see it that way, the question "where does purpose come from" and the question "where does life come from" and the question "where does computation come from in the physical world" all start looking like the same question.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to distinguish purpose as something imposed from outside from purpose that emerges within a system. In BFF, we’re not giving the programs a task and rewarding them for doing it. We have a population of little programs that interact and modify one another. The interesting transition is when those interactions produce self-replication.

Once something can make more of itself, you get a kind of historical filtering. Things that persist and reproduce become more prevalent, and things that don’t disappear. That gives you the beginnings of a distinction between what’s good and bad for an entity. A particular interaction can help it continue to exist, or prevent it from doing so. There’s now a sense in which something matters to that entity, even though we haven’t supplied an explicit objective function.

I wouldn’t equate that with conscious intention. The program doesn’t have to be thinking, ‘I want to survive.’ But it gives us a way to understand how apparently purposeful organization can arise from dynamics that have no foresight. Purpose, in that sense, is something we should be trying to explain, rather than something we have to put in at the beginning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to distinguish purpose that somebody puts into a system from purpose that emerges within it. In BFF, we have these little programs interacting in a computational environment. We haven’t given them a reward function that says, “You should reproduce.” Yet self-reproduction can emerge out of those interactions.

Once something reproduces, you have the beginnings of a very different dynamic. Variations that contribute to continued reproduction tend to persist, and variations that don’t tend to disappear. That gives you a direction without requiring foresight. Nothing has to understand the future for its behavior to become organized around an outcome.

That’s the sense in which I think purpose begins to appear. You can start to explain a piece of the system in terms of what it does for the persistence of the whole. That doesn’t mean it’s conscious, or that it has intentions in the human sense. But it gives us a way to understand how apparently goal-directed behavior can arise from interactions that weren’t goal-directed to begin with.
